hero.title: Polarization
hero.lead: 2-8 Polarization: its definition, the methods of obtaining polarized light, and its applications

objectives: Defines polarized light and distinguishes it from ordinary (unpolarized) light.
Explains why only transverse waves — not longitudinal waves — can be polarized.
States the three methods of obtaining polarized light.
States practical applications of the phenomenon of polarization.

content.label: 📌 2-8 Polarization
content.html: Since light waves are electromagnetic waves and undergo interference and diffraction as covered previously, there is a phenomenon that occurs only for transverse waves and not for longitudinal waves — this phenomenon is polarization, which proves that the electric-field wave of light vibrates perpendicular to the magnetic field, in a single plane only.

content.svgAriaLabel: Simulation of an electromagnetic wave with two perpendicular fields
content.sectionHeading: 🕹️ Recreating Figure 2-12: The Electric and Magnetic Fields in an Electromagnetic Wave
content.descriptionHtml: An electromagnetic wave moving to the right: the electric field (red) vibrates vertically, and the magnetic field (blue) vibrates horizontally, and both are perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation and to each other.

content.html: We can picture polarization as follows: if we imagine transverse waves created in a shaken rope, these waves will take on several directions — such waves are called unpolarized waves. But suppose this shaken rope passes through a vertical slit; this slit will stop all the horizontal components and allow only the vertical components to pass through it, so the resulting wave through it is called a polarized wave.

content.label: 📌 Definition of Polarized Light
content.html: The polarized light wave can be defined as the wave in which the vibration of the electric field is perpendicular, in a single plane only, to its direction of propagation, which is caused by its incidence on a plate called the polarizing plate.

To prove that a wave is transverse, all you need is to demonstrate its ability to be polarized. A longitudinal wave — such as sound waves, whose particles oscillate along the same line as the wave's propagation — cannot be polarized.

content.svgAriaLabel: Simulation of light passing through two polarizing filters at a variable angle
content.sectionHeading: 🕹️ Interactive Simulation: Two Polarizing Filters (Figures 2-13 and 2-14)
content.descriptionHtml: Unpolarized light first passes through a first polarizing filter (making it vertically polarized), then through a second filter (the analyzer) at an angle θ that you can rotate. Notice how the intensity of the transmitted light changes with the analyzer's angle.

content.label: 📌 1- Polarization by Selective Absorption
content.html: Such as using a tourmaline crystal, which has the property of selectively absorbing one of the two perpendicular components of the light wave.

content.label: 📌 2- Polarization by Reflection
content.html: Light reflected from a polished surface — such as glass or mica — is partially polarized.

content.label: 📌 3- Polarization by Double Refraction
content.html: When a light beam falls on a calcite crystal \((\text{CaCO}_3)\), the beam splits inside the crystal into two beams, and these two beams do not interfere despite being similar; this proves that light is a transverse wave, because the plane of polarization of one beam is perpendicular to that of the other.

content.heading: 📋 Some Practical Applications of Polarization
items: Sunglasses (to reduce the transmission of sunlight).
In the study of astronomical phenomena.
In the study of the crystalline properties of certain materials.
Studying the composition of many transparent materials using polarizing filters.
Detecting stress locations (points of weakness) in certain materials, such as eyeglass lenses and practical tools.

content.html: Polarized lenses in sunglasses allow only a limited part of the bright light to pass through, thereby reducing the intensity of light reaching the eye.

questions.question: The phenomenon of polarization occurs only in:
options: Longitudinal waves only
Sound waves only
Transverse waves, not longitudinal ones
All types of waves without exception
questions.explain: Polarization is a phenomenon that occurs only for transverse waves (like light), and does not occur for longitudinal waves (like sound).

questions.question: Polarized light is light in which the vibration of:
options: The magnetic field only, in all directions
The electric field is perpendicular, in a single plane only, to the direction of wave propagation
The electric field is in all random directions
The particles is along the direction of wave propagation itself
questions.explain: Polarized light: in it, the electric field vibrates perpendicular, in a single plane only, to the direction of wave propagation.

questions.question: When a light beam falls on a calcite crystal (CaCO₃), it:
options: Vanishes completely
Reflects at a single angle only
Fully transforms into a longitudinal wave
Splits into two beams with perpendicular polarization that do not interfere
questions.explain: Double refraction in a calcite crystal splits the light beam into two beams, the plane of polarization of one perpendicular to the other, which is evidence of the transverse nature of the light wave.

questions.question: Light reflected from a polished surface such as glass is:
options: Partially polarized
Not polarized at all
Fully 100% polarized
Zero intensity
questions.explain: Polarization by reflection from a polished surface (such as glass or mica) produces only partially polarized light.

questions.question: Among the practical applications of polarization:
options: Measuring the temperature of objects remotely
Sunglasses and detecting stress locations in transparent materials
Generating electrical energy
Accelerating subatomic particles
questions.explain: Applications of polarization include: sunglasses, the study of astronomical phenomena, biology, and crystalline properties, and detecting stress locations in transparent materials.

summary.heading: 📋 Lesson Summary
items: Polarization is a phenomenon that proves the transverse nature of light, and does not occur in longitudinal waves.
Polarized light: the electric field vibrates in a single plane only, perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
Methods of obtaining polarized light: selective absorption (tourmaline), reflection (glass/mica), double refraction (calcite).
Its applications: sunglasses, astronomy, biology, the study of crystals and transparent materials, and stress detection.
